Linn County at a glance

Cedar Rapids is both the biggest city and the seat of Linn County, which lies in eastern Iowa. The county's 230,299 people (2020 count) make it the second most populous in the state.

After Cedar Rapids at 137,710, the biggest cities are Marion at 41,535, Hiawatha at 7,183, Mount Vernon at 4,527 and Robins at 3,353.

Selling here starts with one practical question: which assessor covers your house? The answer changes at the Cedar Rapids city line, and the next section sorts it out.

Which office handles what

Inside Cedar Rapids, the City Assessor values your house. Outside the city limits, the Linn County Assessor takes over. Neither one collects tax or sets the rate. The City Assessor's office says as much itself, and the county assessor's work is likewise about value, with taxing bodies setting budgets and levies. The state Department of Revenue, not either local office, values utilities and railroads.

  • Linn County Assessor (linn.iowaassessors.com): values real property and revalues in odd-numbered years, so every second year. Its assessment date is January 1.
  • Cedar Rapids City Assessor (500 15th Avenue SW, 319-286-5888): covers property inside the city and revalues annually.
  • Linn County Treasurer (935 Second St. SW, 319-892-5500): takes payments, conducts the tax sale and processes redemptions.
  • Board of Review: hears protests. It has five members chosen by the Conference Board, and you reach it through the assessor's office.

Property tax calendar

Value is fixed on January 1, tax comes due in two installments, and protest season is April.

A spring payment needs a March 31 postmark and a fall payment needs September 30. Interest on a delinquent installment is 1.5 percent monthly.

How to protest your assessment

Your written protest must reach the Board of Review from April 2 through April 30 in the assessment year, and the board cannot extend that window. Declared disaster areas are the lone exception, with filing from May 1 to June 5 (Iowa Code 441.37).

Pick from five statutory grounds:

  • Similar property in your taxing district is assessed lower.
  • Your value exceeds what the law allows.
  • The property is not assessable, is exempt, or is classified wrongly.
  • The assessor made an error.
  • Fraud or misconduct occurred, and you must describe it specifically.

An oral hearing happens only if you request it, in writing, at the time you file. If several parcels share the same grounds, a single form can cover them. When the board rules, it sends written notice of what it did and why.

Paying your bill

You can pay online, by mail, in a drop box, by phone, or at the counter of the Treasurer at 935 Second St. SW, Cedar Rapids. Checks are written to the Linn County Treasurer. Send the stub torn from your statement along with the check so it posts to the correct parcel.

  • Paying cash or a check at the counter adds no fee.
  • Online, checks cost $0.30, debit cards cost $3.25 plus $0.30 a transaction, and credit cards cost 2.20 percent plus $0.30 a transaction.
  • Cash cannot be paid online.
  • Lobby hours are Monday through Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4 p.m., except the second Wednesday of each month, when the lobby opens at 10 a.m.

Watch the mail. USPS now postmarks an envelope on the day it is processed, not the day you drop it off, so a late-processed letter can count as late. A manual postmark from a staffed retail counter is free and protects you. If you are cutting it close on September 30 or March 31, walking the payment into the Treasurer's office or using the drop box removes the postmark question altogether.

What happens to the tax when you sell

An unpaid installment does not vanish when the house changes hands, so it gets settled at closing. The current installment is split the way your purchase contract says. Delinquent amounts come out of what you receive, leaving the buyer with title free of them.

In practice the order of events is simple. Call the Treasurer for a balance before listing and pass that figure to the title company. The payoff then appears on your settlement statement. When you meet the closing agent, take your latest tax statement and any delinquency notice so nobody has to guess. Ask also whether any tax suspension or clearance letter applies to your parcel, since those can affect the closing date.

The Treasurer's office also issues plat and mobile home clearances and processes tax suspensions, which can come up around a sale. The state transfer tax is 80 cents per $500 of value beyond the first $500, and it falls on the seller as grantor (Iowa Code 428A.1 and 428A.3).

If taxes are far behind

Taxes that stay unpaid long enough are offered at the June tax sale. The Treasurer conducts it, processes redemptions and issues the tax sale deeds. To get a sold parcel back you pay the sold amount plus 2 percent interest per month. Our statewide Iowa tax deed and tax lien sales guide walks through the redemption steps.

Cash Home Buyers buys Linn County houses as-is, including ones with tax issues, and we confirm numbers with you before any offer. A cash sale avoids repairs and showings, and back taxes are paid from the price at closing. If you are sitting on several years of unpaid installments, tell us up front. The sooner the real balance is known, the sooner you can decide between redeeming, listing, or selling for cash, and the June sale date is the clock that matters most.

Older Cedar Rapids houses and past damage

On June 13, 2008 the Cedar River peaked at a record 31.12 feet, and on August 10, 2020 a derecho hit the county. Cedar Rapids housing still shows both. An older house may carry history from repairs made after either one.

If yours does, gather permits, contractor invoices and insurance paperwork before you talk to any buyer. Paperwork like this answers a traditional buyer's inspector quickly. An as-is cash buyer will take the house in its present condition and skip the repair haggling.

Frequently asked questions

Who assesses property in Cedar Rapids?

The Cedar Rapids City Assessor, from the City Services Center at 500 15th Avenue SW. The Linn County Assessor covers real property in the rest of the county.

When are Linn County property taxes due?

The first half is due September 1 and payable through September 30. The second half is due March 1 and payable through March 31. Payments must be postmarked by those dates.

What is the deadline to protest a Linn County assessment?

April 30 of the assessment year, with filing opening April 2. Declared disaster areas get May 1 through June 5.

What late interest applies in Linn County?

Delinquent installments accrue 1.5 percent interest per month. A payment that arrives without a valid postmark can also draw a 1.5 percent late fee.

Where do I call the Linn County Treasurer?

Call 319-892-5500, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Hold times can be long, so a visit or an appointment at the Public Service Center is sometimes faster.

Scott County at a glance

Along the Mississippi in eastern Iowa, Scott County belongs to the Quad Cities metro. Davenport, with 101,724 residents in 2020, is both seat and biggest city. Bettendorf comes next at 39,102, then Eldridge (6,726), LeClaire (4,710), Park View (2,709), Durant (1,871), Blue Grass (1,666), Walcott (1,551), Buffalo (1,176) and Princeton (923).

Every community has its own schools and city services, so bills can differ noticeably from address to address. Know exactly where your house sits before you compare your bill with a neighbor's.

Which assessor covers your house

Two assessors share the work here. Everything outside the City of Davenport belongs to the Scott County Assessor, and Davenport keeps its own City Assessor. You can find both on the fifth floor of the Scott County Administrative Center in Davenport.

Owners in Bettendorf, Eldridge or a rural township deal with the county assessor, while owners inside Davenport deal with the city assessor. A single records search on the county site covers assessor, auditor and treasurer files by name, address or parcel number, and Davenport City Assessor files are included. Read your parcel record before calling, and you will reach the correct office on the first try. That saves a transfer between two offices on the same floor.

Appealing your assessment

Under Iowa Code 441.37, assessment protests go to the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30. The assessor for your parcel can explain how to file. Ask also whether an informal review is available first, since that can resolve a disagreement without a formal hearing.

Due dates and how to pay

Two equal installments make up the yearly bill: September 30, and March 31 of the following year. When a due date falls on a weekend or holiday, it shifts to the next business day. The county certifies taxes in July or August.

Interest begins the first business day after a due date, which makes a payment one day late delinquent already. Call the Treasurer for today's rate before you work out a payoff.

There are two Treasurer locations in Davenport. One is the Scott County Administrative Center, 600 W. 4th St. The other is the Scott County General Store, 902 W. Kimberly Rd., Suite 6D. Mailed payments go to 600 W 4th St, Davenport, IA 52801-1003. Each has a drop box for checks, and people with appointments get priority.

When taxes go unpaid

Each June the county publishes its delinquent taxes and sells them at a tax sale on the third Monday of the month. A buyer gets a certificate. After two publications with no buyer, the certificate goes to Scott County. Taxes that are never redeemed within the legal period can end in a deed for the certificate holder, and properties the county holds are usually auctioned.

For an owner who has fallen behind, the calendar is the thing to watch:

  • September 30 and March 31 are the due dates, and interest can begin the next business day.
  • June is when delinquent parcels are published.
  • The third Monday of June is the sale.
  • Redemption stays open until the legal period runs out.

A sale completed before the tax sale date takes the lien off your title. Cash buyers can often close quickly enough to pay the county from the proceeds. Just get the exact payoff from the Treasurer first.

Recording the deed

A deed missing any required statement or block is refused by the Scott County Recorder, and sellers and closing agents regularly overlook a few.

  • A Declaration of Value, required for deeds, contracts, assignments of contracts and quit claim deeds unless the document is exempt.
  • Transfer (revenue) tax on the full sale price over $500, or a stated exemption on the face of the document under Iowa Code chapter 428A.2.
  • A groundwater hazard statement, or a sentence saying the transaction is exempt. Since July 1, 2022, a seller may skip the statement if none of the listed conditions exist on the property.
  • A Prepared by block with name, address and telephone, plus an Address tax statement block with name, address and zip code, placed below the blank space required at the top of the page.
  • A complete legal description.

Accuracy of the groundwater statement is the owner's responsibility. Realtors and attorneys can answer questions, and the form itself is posted by the Iowa Department of Natural Resources.

Getting ready to sell, step by step

Begin with the parcel record. Look yourself up by address in the county records search, note whether the county or the Davenport City Assessor holds the file, and print the page. Next, ask the Treasurer for a payoff covering every installment and any tax sale certificate. If you are close to April, ask the right assessor how to file a protest, because a lower value changes what you owe.

Then line up the recording items. Your closing agent will need a complete legal description, the name and address for the Prepared by and Address tax statement blocks, and a decision on the groundwater statement or its exemption sentence. Settling those details before you accept an offer keeps the Recorder from bouncing the deed and delaying your closing. If you own more than one parcel, repeat the payoff request for each one, since a certificate on a second parcel can hold up the deal just as easily as the first.

How a cash sale works with taxes due

Title work in a cash sale matches any other sale, except that no lender or appraisal is involved. Those two are common causes of delay.

Before closing, the closing agent checks the Treasurer's record for unpaid installments and any tax sale certificate. An open installment is paid from your proceeds. If a certificate has been issued, its holder must be paid and released before the deed can clear.

Some situations come up often in Scott County:

  • An inherited Davenport house with the last installment unpaid and nobody living in it.
  • A rental in a river-town neighborhood with deferred repairs that make a bank appraisal difficult.
  • A house split between two heirs in different states who cannot agree on repairs.

If one of these sounds like yours, send us the address and a short note about the tax status. We will tell you whether the parcel is in the county or the Davenport assessment system and what we need to see before we write an offer.

Frequently asked questions

Who sends the property tax bill in Scott County?

The Scott County Treasurer collects property tax for the county, cities, schools and other taxing bodies. Assessments come from the Scott County Assessor, or from the Davenport City Assessor if the house is inside Davenport.

What are the Scott County property tax due dates?

The first installment is due September 30 and the second is due March 31 of the following year. A date on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day.

Can I pay Scott County property tax online?

Yes. The Treasurer accepts e-checks and credit cards online, with a $0.25 e-check fee and a 2.25% credit card fee. Cash and debit cards are not accepted online.

When is the Scott County tax sale?

The annual tax sale is held on the third Monday of June, and delinquent taxes are published in June before that date.

Can I sell a Scott County house with unpaid property tax?

Yes. Unpaid taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at closing. Get a current payoff from the Treasurer before you accept any offer so you know how much will be deducted.

Dallas County market context

Dallas County sits just west of Des Moines, with Adel as seat and Waukee as the largest city. Few places grow like this one: 66,135 residents in 2010, 99,678 in 2020, and an estimated 118,457 in 2025. Median home value is $355,600, 69.0 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and median household income is $102,379. Waukee alone climbed from 5,126 people in 2000 to 23,940 in 2020.

Addresses can mislead. West Des Moines lies mostly in Polk County, so a house with that mailing city might be billed by either county. Look up the parcel record to see who taxes it.

County offices and phone numbers

Most property offices share the Administration Building, 800 Court Street, Adel, and a second county location operates in Perry. The courthouse itself is listed at 801 Court Street.

  • Treasurer, Tax Division: 800 Court Street, Suite 111, first floor. Phone 515-993-5808, email propertytax@dallascountyiowa.gov.
  • Assessor: 515-993-5802.
  • Auditor: 515-993-6914. Builds levy rates out of local budgets.
  • Recorder: 800 Court Street, Suite 130. Phone 515-993-5804, open Monday to Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., with an online record search and a transfer tax calculator.

Payment dates and penalties

Your tax comes in two parts. The fall part is due September 1 and turns delinquent once September 30 passes. The spring part is due March 1 and turns delinquent after March 31. Statements reach mailboxes in August.

A late payment accrues 1.5 percent per month, rounded to the dollar. As proof of mailing, the county honors only a U.S. Postal Service postmark. Neither the date on your check nor a postage meter date counts, so have a clerk at the post office stamp the envelope while you stand there.

Dallas County property tax calendar

September 1First half due
March 1Second half due
Third Monday in JuneAnnual county tax sale
June 1Senior and disabled credit applications due
September 30Special assessment credit claim due

A statement that never came does not excuse a late payment. Newcomers should call for a copy, and anyone with a lender should confirm the lender has the correct parcel data.

The June tax sale

Each year the treasurer conducts the auction, set for the third Monday of June unless the office picks another day. Redemptions, tax sale deeds and suspensions run through the same desk.

A certificate holder can pay later delinquent taxes after November 15 and May 15 if a half is still open. An owner, or anyone with a recorded interest, redeems by paying the sold tax plus 2 percent monthly. When no one does, the lien may end in a tax deed.

Assessments and protests

The assessor values each parcel on a January 1 snapshot, and the Iowa cycle needs about 18 months before that value shows on a bill. Value as of January 2026, for example, produces the fall 2027 and spring 2028 payments.

The Board of Review takes protests from April 2 through April 30 (Iowa Code 441.37). Your case can rest on unequal treatment, an overstated value, a wrong exemption or class, a mistake, or fraud. Deadlines are firm, except in federal disaster counties, where the window can move to May 1 through June 5.

A state equalization order opens one more protest period, October 9 to October 31, and the only argument allowed is that the order raised value beyond Iowa Code 441.21. Appeals continue to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court, and you have 20 days from adjournment.

Homestead exemption changes

Under Senate File 2472, signed May 18, 2026, the homestead credit is replaced by an exemption: 10 percent of taxable value, at least $5,500 and at most $20,000. It begins with assessment year 2026 and first shows on the September 2027 and March 2028 bills.

Existing claimants stay enrolled, and the disabled veteran credit remains. Anyone buying applies on their own. Eligibility questions go to the Department of Revenue's property tax division at 515-281-3114.

Taxes and recording at closing

At most closings the buyer receives a credit for the seller's part of this year's tax, and the Recorder in Adel files the deed.

Iowa's transfer tax comes to 80 cents for each $500 past the first $500. A declaration of value, signed by a seller, buyer or agent, travels with every deed and stays with the assessor for three years from December 31 of the transfer year. Your sales contract settles who pays.

Steps before you list

Start by calling the Treasurer's Tax Division at 515-993-5808 for the amount owed on each half, plus accrued interest through your planned closing date if a half is late. Confirm the parcel number matches your deed, especially if your mailing address sounds like a different city. Next, ask the assessor at 515-993-5802 which credits are attached to the house. The Recorder's transfer tax calculator shows that cost before you set a price. Armed with those answers, the title company orders a payoff and closing avoids late surprises. Houses that need work can also sell for cash as-is, which keeps every tax step above but trims the rest of the timeline.

Why timing matters for a seller

Because value takes about 18 months to reach a bill, the tax you pay this year reflects an assessment from the year before last. A seller in a fast-growing county can face a valuation that lags behind sale prices, and a buyer may ask what the next reassessment will do. The assessor at 515-993-5802 can say when your parcel's next valuation lands, which helps you answer that question honestly. Odd or even year, the protest window is the same: April 2 to April 30.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Special credits to know about

Two deadlines in the calendar above deserve attention. Senior and disabled credit applications are due June 1, and a special assessment credit claim is due September 30. If you hold either, mention it to the title company so the closing statement accounts for it, and tell the buyer that a fresh application is theirs to file. Missing a credit date does not usually stop a sale, but it can cost the next owner a year of savings.

If your house is in Perry or a smaller town

Sellers outside the metro suburbs have the same obligations as those in Waukee: the same two payment dates, the same assessor, and the same June auction. The difference is mostly in the buyer pool, which is smaller, so a clean tax record helps a listing move. Before you advertise, pay any open half, get a letter or printout of the balance for the title company, and keep the postmarked proof of payment. If an old statement went to a lender or to a deceased owner, call the treasurer so the right person receives the next one.

Frequently asked questions

When are Dallas County property taxes due?

Fall half September 1, spring half March 1. Once September 30 or March 31 passes, 1.5 percent a month is added.

Where is the Dallas County Treasurer?

Visit Suite 111 at 800 Court Street in Adel, or call 515-993-5808.

When is the Dallas County tax sale?

June, normally the third Monday, with the treasurer free to choose another date.

How do I protest my Dallas County assessment?

Send a written petition to the Board of Review during April 2 to April 30, then, if needed, take the ruling to the appeal board or district court.

Do Dallas County owners need to refile for the new homestead exemption?

No. People already claiming the credit stay enrolled, while a new owner files separately.

Buchanan County at a glance

Northeast Iowa holds Buchanan County. Independence serves as seat and biggest city, home to 6,064 people in 2020, while the whole county totaled 20,565 and roughly 67 percent of residents live outside towns. Expect plenty of acreage and farm parcels among the listings, and remember that a bill is attached to the parcel, not the owner.

Payment calendar

Two installments make up the year here. September 1 is the date for the first and March 1 for the second, and each has a grace period that ends on the last day of that month. Paying everything at once is allowed.

Bills go out in August. A deadline that lands on a Saturday or Sunday slides to the following business day. Once a half goes delinquent, in October or April, interest accrues at 1.5 percent monthly, rounded to the whole dollar, never less than $1.

Protesting an assessment

The board of review hears protests from April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year. Under Iowa Code section 441.37 you may argue only one of five things: unequal treatment next to similar property, a value over the legal limit, wrong classification or an exemption you should have, a mistake in the record, or fraud.

Expect a written ruling that explains itself. Anyone still unhappy can take the matter to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or file in district court. Phone the assessor to learn when the next reassessment falls and whether informal reviews begin before April 2 passes.

That same office handles homestead, veteran and family farm credit sign-ups, and a credit can shrink a bill without any appeal.

If taxes go unpaid

Each June, delinquent parcels go up for bid at the county sale, normally the third Monday. The winning bidder covers the overdue tax, and to get the parcel back an owner repays that sum along with 2 percent for every month that has gone by.

The website will not take a redemption. Dial the treasurer at 319-334-4340 instead. Let the redemption period lapse and the bidder can begin the road to a deed. For a house you intend to sell, clearing the debt first is cheaper, because a sold certificate piles interest and fees onto the payoff.

Transfer tax

Sellers owe Iowa's real estate transfer tax, set at 80 cents on each $500 of value past the first $500. The county recorder takes the money. A declaration of value must come in with the deed, and without it the recorder will not record.

Iowa Code section 428A.2 exempts certain transfers: gifts between spouses or between a parent and child, inheritances passed without payment, and tax deeds. An ordinary full-price sale is taxable. The state sends 82.75 percent of monthly receipts to the Department of Revenue, and the county general fund keeps what remains.

Houses here are often in small towns or on country ground, so fewer shoppers compete for them than in a city. Inherited homes and places with postponed repairs are the usual reasons owners consider a fast sale.

  • Confirm the parcel's county first, since Jesup and Fairbank cross county lines.
  • Ask the treasurer what is still owed on each half.
  • See whether a homestead, veteran or family farm credit is attached to the parcel at the assessor's office.
  • Have the deed ready so the declaration of value goes in at recording.

When a property needs repairs or the taxes are behind, selling for cash as-is avoids a buyer's lender, appraiser and inspection list, so the sale can close sooner than a listing would.

A simple closing sequence

A few days before the closing date, phone the treasurer and ask what each half currently costs, interest included. The title company subtracts that total from your proceeds. Next, the deed and declaration of value reach the recorder, who collects the transfer tax. Let the assessor know about the sale so a homestead or veteran credit does not linger on a house that has changed hands. Hang on to your settlement statement. It shows how the present year's bill was divided between you and the buyer, which matters if the county later sends a corrected notice. Anyone selling a rural parcel should also check the parcel number on the deed against the tax record, since acreage splits can leave two numbers in play.

Back taxes before a sale

Suppose a parent's house in Independence is headed for sale and nobody has opened the mail for a while. Start by asking the treasurer for the balance on both halves. If either half is delinquent, interest is already running at 1.5 percent a month. If the parcel was sold at the June auction, the cost to redeem climbs by 2 percent each month until the owner pays. Either way, the title company will want a written figure good through the closing date, and the sum comes out of the seller's proceeds. Heirs selling an inherited house follow the same path, and a transfer to heirs without payment is one of the exempt transfers listed above, so the recorder should not charge transfer tax on that step.

Do not wait for the next statement to settle this. A house with an open balance can stall at the title stage, and a buyer's attorney will ask for proof the tax is current.

Questions for the assessor

A short call to the assessor can save a surprise. Ask which credits are on the parcel and whether any need to be removed after you sell. Ask when informal reviews open in April, since a quick conversation may fix an error before you need a formal protest. Ask what year the next reassessment falls in, because a buyer may want to know whether the value is about to change. And if you own farm ground, ask how the family farm credit is handled when the land passes to a new owner.

Pay by September 30 for the first half and March 31 for the second. Interest of 1.5 percent a month starts after those dates.

Where do I pay Buchanan County property tax?

Go to the treasurer on the first floor of the courthouse at 210 5th Avenue NE in Independence, or pay online at pay.iowataxandtags.org. The tax line is 319-334-4340.

When is the Buchanan County tax sale?

Each June, usually the third Monday. The treasurer may pick another date.

How do I contest my Buchanan County assessment?

Send a protest to the board of review in April, from April 2 to April 30, citing one of the five grounds in Iowa Code section 441.37.

Does Iowa charge a transfer tax when I sell?

Yes, 80 cents per $500 above the first $500. The seller owes it, and the recorder collects it along with a declaration of value.

Dubuque County overview

Three states meet near Dubuque County, which borders the Mississippi in Iowa's far east. The city of Dubuque is the seat and the biggest place, and the whole county held 99,266 people in 2020, ninth highest in Iowa. After the city come Asbury (5,943), Dyersville (4,477), Cascade (2,386), Epworth (2,023), Peosta (1,908) and Farley (1,766).

Hills and woods mark the east, farmland the west. Whether your house is on a bluff street or a farm near Cascade, the same courthouse offices handle your valuation and your bill.

Who collects and who values

Checks go to the Dubuque County Treasurer. The City of Dubuque states that it neither bills nor collects property tax, and the county forwards the city's portion every month.

You can book a treasurer appointment online and avoid waiting in line, and the county home page carries a Beacon lookup for property records. One caution: Dubuque also employs a city assessor, so a parcel inside the city may be valued by that office instead of the county. A call to the courthouse with your parcel number clears it up.

Payment calendar

The statewide Iowa schedule governs. Your first installment is due September 1 and your second March 1, and each may be paid through the last day of its month.

  • August brings the statements, mailed once the county auditor certifies the levy.
  • Deadlines are September 30 and March 31, sliding to the next business day when they land on a weekend.
  • October is when an unpaid fall half turns delinquent, and April for the spring half.
  • A delinquent installment accrues 1.5 percent monthly, with a one dollar floor.

Iowa bills lag by a year. September and March payments cover the fiscal year that closed the previous June 30, so you may owe for a stretch when the house was yours even if the buyer takes possession before the bill is mailed.

Not getting a statement erases nothing. It is on the owner to see that a bill arrives and gets paid, and a parcel number is enough to make a payment.

The June tax sale

Each June, normally on the third Monday, the county auctions parcels with unpaid tax online at iowataxauction.com, and bidders sign up beforehand. One recent publication notice named about 450 real estate parcels and about 130 mobile homes, with amounts due from $6 to $104,077 including penalty and costs.

  • To redeem, you pay 2 percent per month on the sale amount, and a part month is billed as a whole one.
  • After a regular sale, the 90-day notice of right of redemption can issue once one year and nine months run from the sale date.
  • After a public bidder sale, the same notice can issue at nine months.
  • A redemption counts only when the treasurer has it before close of business on the 90th day after service is complete.

An asterisk beside a parcel in the notice means it has been advertised for two years with no buyer. When nobody bids privately, the county bids what is owed. If you hold such a parcel and want to sell, talk with the treasurer before the next June auction.

Valuation and appeals

Assessors start from full market value for homes, and a state rollback percentage trims it to taxable value. The rollback shifts each year, and taxable growth on existing homes statewide is capped at 3 percent. The county reassesses in odd-numbered years, and the Department of Revenue may order an adjustment when a class lands outside a 95 to 105 percent ratio band.

If you think your value is wrong, file a written protest with the Board of Review from April 2 to April 30 of the assessment year. Iowa Code 441.37 gives five grounds:

  • unequal treatment compared with similar property;
  • a value above what the law permits;
  • wrong classification, or a property that should be exempt;
  • an error in the assessment;
  • fraud or misconduct, which must be spelled out.

Ask for a hearing in writing when you file. A written ruling with reasons comes back. Still disagree? The Property Assessment Appeal Board, reachable at 515-725-0338, or district court is the next stop.

Slopes, creeks and age

Buyers tend to ask about three physical things first: how steep the lot is, whether water reaches it, and how old the systems are. Bluffs shape many Dubuque lots, and low ground by the river and creeks carries flood risk. Aging houses frequently need a new roof, rewiring, foundation work or a sewer line repair before a conventional buyer's inspector is satisfied.

Selling for cash as-is sidesteps that repair list. Even then, check taxes and special assessments with the treasurer before you commit to a date.

What changes hands at closing

Closings usually prorate the year's tax on the statement, either crediting the buyer for the seller's portion or having the seller pay the treasurer directly. If you close from July 1 through December 31, the September installment is yours. Close from January 1 through June 30 and the March installment is yours.

  • Delinquent tax and any sold amounts must be cleared before the title can pass cleanly.
  • A deed for more than $500 carries state transfer tax at 80 cents per $500, or fraction, above $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1).
  • The buyer or seller signs a declaration of value, which goes to the recorder with the deed and then to the assessor, who keeps it for three years.

Since those declarations reach the assessor, your price may later be cited when someone studies values nearby. Keep the settlement statement for your records.

Checklist for an owner about to list

Call the courthouse and ask whether your parcel is valued by the county or the city assessor. Request the balance on each half, with interest to your target closing date. Look at the sale notice to see whether the parcel is flagged. Book an appointment online if you would rather not wait. Then hand the figures to the title company so the payoff is ready for the table. If a notice is already out, the delinquent tax, penalty and costs come off your proceeds, and the treasurer can confirm the final number a day or two before closing. Sellers who inherit a house should also ask how long any redemption period still has to run, since that decides how much time there is to act.

Frequently asked questions

Who do I pay property tax to in Dubuque County?

Pay the Dubuque County Treasurer at the courthouse, 720 Central Avenue. The City of Dubuque does not collect it.

What happens if I miss the September 30 payment in Dubuque County?

The first half turns delinquent in October and picks up 1.5 percent a month, never under one dollar. If it stays open, the parcel can be listed for the June sale.

Can I sell a Dubuque County house that is on the tax sale list?

Yes. The overdue tax, penalty and costs are normally paid from your proceeds at closing, and a sold certificate adds 2 percent a month on the sale amount.

When can I protest my Dubuque County assessment?

April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year, in writing, to the Board of Review.

Which payment does a seller owe, September or March?

Close between July 1 and December 31 and you owe September. Close between January 1 and June 30 and you owe March.

Monona County at a glance

Western Iowa's Monona County runs along the Missouri River, and Onawa is both its seat and its biggest town. In 2020 the census found 8,751 residents across 694 square miles of land, roughly 12.5 per square mile. Numbers topped out near 17,980 around 1900 and have slid since 1940. Most sales are small-town houses or rural parcels with extra ground. After generations of shrinking, replacement cost is a poor guide, so set your price from recent recorded sales close by.

After Onawa (2,906) come Mapleton (1,165), Whiting (745), Ute (338), Blencoe (233), Moorhead (199), Soldier (184), Castana (107), Turin (72) and Rodney (45). Several are tiny, which can leave a house in one of them with few recent comparable sales.

Slopes, soil and river flooding

Much of the county, Onawa included, lies in the Loess Hills, a ridge of wind-blown silt beside the Missouri River. The soil, called sugar clay, hardens when dry but loses cohesion when wet, so slopes can slump. A lot on a hillside or beside a cut bank will draw close attention to drainage and foundation movement from a buyer's inspector.

The river matters too. In the 2019 floods, Missouri River flooding lasted as long as seven months in some places, and stretches of I-29 in western Iowa were closed. The hardest-hit area was the valley south of Council Bluffs, not Monona County, but a seller on or near the floodplain should have flood insurance history and repair records ready.

Disasters also change the tax calendar. A disaster declaration made after March 1 and before May 20 pushes the protest deadline from April 30 to June 5, and lets the board of review keep sitting until June 15.

Who collects property tax

Bills are collected by the county Treasurer, while values come from the county assessor. You will find the Treasurer on the first floor of 610 Iowa Avenue, Onawa, and by mail at P.O. Box 415.

How properties are valued

Real property gets a fresh assessment every odd-numbered year, effective January 1. Each parcel lands in one of five classes: residential, multi-residential, commercial, industrial or agricultural.

Productivity sets the value of farmland, while farm dwellings are valued differently. When you sell a farm, ask which portion of the property counts as the house and which as land, because each is valued its own way.

How to protest your assessment

Informal review requests are accepted April 2 to April 25, and written protests are due April 30. After that, the board of review sits starting May 1 until its work is done.

  • April 2 to 25: talk it over with the assessor.
  • April 2 to 30: file in writing with the board of review.
  • May 1 onward: hearings, which must wrap up by May 31 unless extended.
  • October 9 to 31 of odd years: protests for property affected by a state equalization order.

The board may leave an assessment alone, raise it or cut it. A losing owner has 20 days from adjournment or May 31, whichever falls later, to take the matter to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court. Put your protest in writing; allowed grounds are in Iowa Code 441.37.

Late interest and the June tax sale

Payment comes in two halves. Half one is delinquent as of October 1, and half two as of April 1. After that date the balance grows by one and one-half percent each month, to the nearest dollar, until you pay.

A parcel that remains unpaid is sold publicly on the third Monday of June under Iowa Code 446.7. Afterward the owner can still redeem for the sale amount plus 2% a month, as section 447.1 explains. Call the Treasurer for the current sale details and dates.

Taxes and paperwork when you sell

Along with the deed, the recorder receives a declaration of value. The state transfer tax is 80 cents per $500 over the first $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1). From the recorder it moves to the assessor, who retains it for three years.

To qualify for the homestead credit an owner must occupy the home on July 1 and for at least six months of the year. If the sale comes before July 1, the buyer applies by July 1. If it comes after, the credit remains attached for that year (rule 701-110.1).

  • Request a payoff figure from the Treasurer ahead of closing.
  • Check whether back taxes sit on more than one parcel, such as a house lot plus a field.
  • Save the receipt that shows the parcel is paid up.

From payoff letter to closing

A sale with taxes owed usually moves in this order. You ask the Treasurer for the balance on each parcel, and you ask the assessor whether the classes and values on the record look right. If something is wrong and the dates allow, you protest before April 30. You then agree on a price and sign a contract that says who pays the second-half tax and the transfer tax. At closing the title company pays what is owed from your proceeds, the deed and declaration of value go to the recorder, and you keep the Treasurer's receipt.

Skipping the first step is the usual mistake. A balance you have not seen can include interest at one and one-half percent a month, and a second parcel you forgot about can hold up the closing for days.

Selling when taxes are behind

Back taxes call for a short sequence. First, phone 712-433-2347, extension 1, and get the exact balance on every parcel. Next, weigh that balance against a realistic sale price. Then choose between a traditional listing and an as-is sale. Under either, the unpaid tax is paid out of your proceeds when you close.

Going the listing route brings repairs, showings and a wait on a buyer's loan. Someone paying cash for the house as it stands cuts those out, which matters when the June sale is near. At your first conversation with any buyer or agent, have the tax statement, past receipts and any records of flood or slope repairs in hand. Doing that early also tells you whether anything else is attached to the parcel before a title company finds it.

Visit the Treasurer at 610 Iowa Avenue, first floor, Onawa, or pay through the Iowa Treasurers parcel page online. Call 712-433-2347, extension 1.

The deadline is April 30, and filing opens April 2. Informal review with the assessor is available April 2 to April 25.

How often are Monona County properties reassessed?

In every odd-numbered year, as of January 1. The assessor determines values and has no say over tax rates.

Yes. Interest is one and one-half percent a month, rounded to the dollar, never less than $1, and a partial month is charged as a whole one.

Clarion became the county seat in 1866, after the seat had been at Liberty since 1858. The courthouse dates from 1891 and 1892 and joined the National Register of Historic Places in 1981. Clarion had 2,810 residents in 2020, down from 2,968 in 2000.

Wright County has six active school districts, including Clarion-Goldfield-Dows, Eagle Grove and Belmond-Klemme. Clarion-Goldfield-Dows took its current form when Dows joined on July 1, 2014. Buena Vista County in brief

Buena Vista County sits in northwest Iowa with Storm Lake as seat and largest city. The 2020 count was 20,823 people, and Storm Lake alone had 11,269 of them. Alta follows with 2,087, then a string of small towns from Newell (906) down to Truesdale (69).

Lakeside, on the east shore of Storm Lake, is its own small city, separate from Storm Lake itself. If your address is by the water, check the parcel record to see which city it falls in, since that affects which levies appear on the bill.

Property tax offices

One office takes the money and the other sets the value, and you reach both at 215 E. 5th Street in Storm Lake. Weekday hours are 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Look for the property tax window on the courthouse's ground level. Payment works through iowatreasurers.org, the mail, a secure box on the building's east side, or a visit in person.

Due dates and penalties

Your bill splits into two halves. Pay the first by September 30. The second can be paid March 1 through March 31. Miss either and a penalty of 1.5 percent per month builds, beginning October 1 for the fall half. A postmark on or before the deadline is accepted, and an online payment counts until 11:59 p.m. that evening. Saturday and Sunday deadlines slide to Monday.

Send the stubs from your statement with a check so it posts to the correct parcel.

  • August: statements are mailed.
  • September 30: first half deadline.
  • March 31: second half deadline.
  • June: annual tax sale of delinquent parcels.

How assessments and appeals work

Real property gets a fresh valuation every other year, the odd-numbered ones, using a January 1 snapshot. Informal review runs April 2 to April 25, and a formal protest to the Board of Review runs April 2 to April 30. In odd years, appeals of an equalization order can be filed October 9 to 31.

Hearings start May 1 and continue until the board adjourns. Members include a farmer, a real estate agent and a person who knows construction. Disagree with the ruling and your options are the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court. A disaster proclamation can stretch these windows to May 25 and June 5.

Homestead exemption and other breaks

Starting with assessment year 2026, the homestead credit became a homestead exemption. It equals 10 percent of the home's taxable value, with a minimum of $5,500 and a maximum of $20,000, and the claim is due by July 1. Those with military service may also qualify for a $4,000 military exemption. The assessor handles both, so call 712-749-2543 if you are unsure what is on your parcel.

Whoever buys the house files their own claim after closing, ideally before July 1 so it starts on the next bill.

Unpaid taxes and the June tax sale

Parcels with unpaid tax go to a yearly auction at the courthouse each June, and all bids are placed online. Redemption cannot be handled through the website. Call 712-749-2533 or visit the treasurer.

To redeem, an owner pays the delinquent tax plus 2 percent for every month since the sale. The county publishes a delinquent tax list every year plus a notice for tax sale purchasers. Scan the list before advertising a house to learn whether the parcel is already queued for June. A payoff number for a chosen closing date is available from the treasurer.

Transfer tax and recording

The seller pays Iowa's transfer tax: 80 cents for every $500 of value past the first $500. Collection happens at the recorder's desk, where a declaration of value accompanies the deed. A few transfers escape it under Iowa Code section 428A.2, including spouse-to-spouse or parent-to-child gifts and estate distributions to heirs that involve no payment.

Owners in Storm Lake, Alta or a smaller town whose taxes or repairs have piled up can look at a cash sale as-is, which closes without a listing or showings. The tax payoff and recording steps still apply.

Preparing to sell

Call the treasurer first. Request a payoff covering both halves plus any penalty through the date you expect to close, then check the delinquent list for your parcel number. Next, contact the assessor about the homestead exemption and any military exemption, because a buyer will want to know what stays and what must be refiled. Then gather the deed so the declaration of value can go in at recording. Once these pieces are collected, the title company can set the closing, deduct the tax from your proceeds, and send the deed to the recorder. Pay attention to your own calendar too: a sale that closes in late spring or summer may fall before the first July 1 claim deadline, which gives the new owner time to file for the exemption.

Walking through a sale with taxes owed

Picture a Storm Lake owner who fell behind on the fall half. Interest has been building since October 1, and if the parcel reaches the June auction it lands on the delinquent list. At that stage the number to learn is the redemption amount, which is the tax sold plus the monthly charge. Ask the treasurer for it in writing with a date the figure stays good, hand it to the title company, and let the closing pay it from your proceeds. Nothing about this blocks a sale. It only adds a line to the settlement statement.

If the parcel has not been sold, the process is shorter: confirm the balance, pay it at closing, and keep the receipt.

Questions to put to the assessor

Call 712-749-2543 and ask which exemptions are on file. Ask whether your parcel is in a reassessment year, because values are reset every two years and a buyer may ask what is coming. Ask when informal review opens, since a short talk in April may settle a disagreement before it needs a formal protest. If the property sits near the lake, ask which city levies apply, and make sure the address on the bill matches the parcel record.

Reading the posted notices

Two postings are worth a look before you list. The delinquent tax list shows which parcels are headed to auction, and the notice to tax sale purchasers describes how bidding works for the year. Neither is an invitation to wait. A parcel that has not been sold can still be cleared with the treasurer at any time, and the earlier you do it the less interest the balance collects, so a quick call is worth making.

Frequently asked questions

When are Buena Vista County property taxes due?

Fall half by September 30, spring half by March 31. After that, 1.5 percent per month is added.

Where do I pay Buena Vista County property tax?

Visit 215 E. 5th Street in Storm Lake, or use iowatreasurers.org, the mail, or the east-side drop box.

How often does Buena Vista County reassess property?

Every second year, the odd ones, with January 1 as the valuation date.

When can I protest my Buena Vista County assessment?

Formal protests go to the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30. An informal review with the assessor is open April 2 to April 25.

Can I redeem a property after the tax sale?

Yes, within the time Iowa law allows. Call the treasurer at 712-749-2533 or visit in person, because redemption cannot be paid through the website.

Mahaska County at a glance

Oskaloosa, with 11,558 residents, is the seat of Mahaska County and dwarfs every other town in it. The whole county held 22,190 people in 2020. After it come New Sharon (1,262), Eddyville (970) and Fremont (708), plus small communities such as Beacon and University Park. The population has hardly changed since 1980, so ownership here is stable and houses tend to change hands slowly.

Hot summers and cold winters wear on older houses, so roofs, furnaces and gutters are where an inspector begins. Think about that when you weigh paying for repairs against selling as-is to a buyer who will handle them. Coal mining once shaped the county, and some rural parcels carry long paper trails. The courthouse holds the deeds and parcel records, so confirm early that you have the right parcel in front of you. That prevents surprises when a title company starts its search.

Who handles property tax

Find both offices in the Mahaska County Courthouse at 106 South 1st Street, Oskaloosa. Value is the Assessor's job, and collection belongs to the Treasurer.

Online, the Assessor page offers Beacon maps and records, a report of recent sales, and a Data Correction Form reachable from any parcel report. Built an addition or lost an outbuilding? Email the office your address and a phone number.

How to challenge your value

Pull up your parcel in Beacon before anything else. From April 2 to April 25 the Assessor will take an informal review request, and the written protest deadline is April 30. The dates are statewide rules found in Iowa Code 441.37 and Department of Revenue guidance.

Use the state form for a written protest, signed by you or your agent. A board may allow electronic filing. Owners can also correct clerical or mathematical errors going back to earlier years, if those years are not fully paid.

  • Aim at the January 1 value, since that is the date assessments reflect.
  • Arguing the value is too high? Bring recent sales close to your house.
  • Claiming the wrong class? Bring proof of how the house is actually used.

What happens after a protest

Protest hearings before the local board of review begin May 1, and the board should finish by May 31. The state may allow more time, though never beyond July 15. Its written decision has to be mailed within three days of adjourning.

If you remain unconvinced, the Property Assessment Appeal Board and district court are the next steps. You have 20 days counted from adjournment or May 31, whichever falls later. Board members serve six-year staggered terms, and at least one must be a farmer (see the Iowa Department of Revenue summary).

Due dates and late interest

Iowa Code chapter 445 makes the first half delinquent October 1 and the second half April 1. A half that is late accrues one and one-half percent interest per month or partial month.

The interest figure is rounded to a whole dollar, and it is never less than $1. Options for paying are the Iowa Treasurers' parcel search online, the courthouse counter, or a mailed check to 106 S 1st Street. Ahead of a closing, phone (641) 673-5482 for exact amounts on your parcel.

The June tax sale

Every June, usually the third Monday, treasurers across Iowa put delinquent parcels up for sale. The buyer covers the taxes, interest, fees and costs. Redemption by the owner afterward takes the sale price, a certificate fee and 2% interest per month (Iowa Code 446.7 and 447.1).

Inherited a house that carries back taxes? Ask the Treasurer about the parcel right away. It is far better to learn the balance now than from a notice after the auction.

Taxes and filings when you sell

The transfer tax works out to 80 cents per $500 of value beyond the first $500. When the deed is filed, a declaration of value accompanies it; the recorder forwards that to the assessor, who retains it three years (Iowa Code 428A.1).

Homestead credit timing can matter to your closing date. When a house sells before July 1, the buyer must claim the credit by July 1. When it sells on or after July 1, the credit remains with the property that year (rule 701-110.1).

  • Tax is a lien on the parcel that ranks ahead of everyone but the state.
  • Tax paid in error can be refunded only if you claim it within two years of the due date.
  • A treasurer's receipt showing full payment is conclusive proof that the parcel was free of taxes.

If you plan to sell in the spring, remember that the January 1 value drives the bill you will split with the buyer. Reading your notice carefully in April, while a protest is still possible, can change what you owe at closing.

Selling with taxes owed, step by step

First, phone the Treasurer at (641) 673-5482 for the balance on your parcel, interest included. Second, read your Beacon parcel report for mistakes in size, class or buildings. If you find one, send the Data Correction Form, and think about a protest when April comes.

Third, choose how to sell. Listing the traditional way means getting the house ready, waiting on a financed buyer and often answering repair requests. Selling as-is for cash skips most of it. Either way, unpaid tax is deducted from the price when you close, the buyer receives the parcel free of it, and the treasurer's receipt documents that. Have the closing agent confirm the payoff figure shortly beforehand, since another month of interest can change it.

Before you list

Pull together three items: a payoff statement, the parcel record and a list of repairs or damage. Together they show how your balance compares with what the house might bring.

  • Pull the Beacon parcel report and use the Data Correction Form for wrong details.
  • Get today's amount from the Treasurer, interest included.
  • For an inherited house, confirm at the courthouse who the owners of record are.
  • See whether the Assessor has a homestead credit on file, and let the buyer know.

Suppose the balance is bigger than you expected or the repair list is long. A cash buyer taking the house as-is can settle the taxes at closing and relieve you of the repairs. Set that offer beside what a listing would net before deciding. Neither choice should be made in a hurry, and the June sale is the date to keep in view.

It opens April 2 and closes April 30 under state law. For an informal review with the Assessor, use April 2 through April 25.

Use the Iowa Treasurers' parcel search online, come to the courthouse on a weekday, or mail payment to 106 S 1st Street. Questions go to (641) 673-5482.

Late interest is one and one-half percent monthly. It rounds to the dollar, never below $1, and part of a month is billed as a whole month.

Which county bills your parcel

Des Moines reaches into Warren County south of County Line Road, so a Des Moines address alone will not tell you who bills the parcel. Settle that question before you request any payoff.

Anyone near the Des Moines or Raccoon rivers should keep flood zone and insurance details handy. Big floods struck downtown in 1993 and 2008, and lenders tend to ask about the zone and your claims history.

Who runs property tax

Valuing and collecting are separate jobs here. The Assessor sets values from 111 Court Avenue, Room 195, Des Moines, IA 50309, phone (515) 286-3014. The Treasurer takes the payments.

Counter service at the Treasurer runs 7:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and there are ways to pay after hours. The same office handles the Senior and Disabled Property Tax Credit, open to owners 65 or older, or totally disabled, within yearly income limits. If you or a parent might qualify, ask about it before you sell, because the credit and its timing can affect the buyer's first bill.

Polk follows the state two-year cycle. Values are refreshed in odd-numbered years. In even years they mostly stay put, apart from changes tied to one property, such as new construction or a demolition. When a value changes, notices go out before April 1.

How to protest your assessment

File a signed written protest from April 2 to April 30, using one form per parcel. Should April 30 land on a weekend, you get the next business day.

  • You may request an informal Assessor review from April 2 through April 25.
  • A signed agreement with the Assessor makes a formal protest unnecessary.
  • Good evidence: an appraisal, recent sales, or three to five comparables.
  • Make your case for the value on the January 1 assessment date, not today's market.

Residential, commercial and agricultural owners each have their own form. A commercial owner may add three years of operating statements and a current rent roll, but nobody requires it. Grounds for protest appear in Iowa Code 441.37, and the Assessor summary walks through the steps.

Preparing a protest, step by step

Keep January 1 in mind, since that is the date your value is tested against. A notice reaches you before April 1 when the value has changed. Compare the new figure with last year's, and if it jumped, gather evidence before you phone anyone. An appraisal carries the most weight, with three to five comparable sales as the common substitute. Note each parcel number, because every parcel gets its own form.

Then try the informal route. In the April 2 to April 25 window the Assessor will go over your numbers with you. A signed agreement at that stage ends the matter and no hearing is needed. If the two of you stay apart, file the formal protest before April 30 and request an oral hearing in the same filing, because that is when you ask for one.

The board of review

The board meets in May and normally wraps up by May 31. An oral hearing is held if you asked for one at filing. The decision, with reasons, arrives in writing.

Owners who lose may turn to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court. The window is 20 days from adjournment or May 31, whichever is later. Unpaid parcels are offered at the yearly sale, which by default falls on the third Monday in June. Recent sales have taken bids online, and the list of properties is printed in the newspaper in early June. Redemption means paying the sale price, fees and 2% interest per month from the month of sale (Iowa Code 447.1).

What happens to tax when you sell

The deed reaches the recorder with a declaration of value attached, and the recorder hands that to the assessor. Transfer tax comes to 80 cents on each $500 above the first $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1). Which side pays is left to your purchase contract, so settle it in writing before you sign and do not assume the buyer or the seller carries it.

  • Have the closing agent say who pays the second-half tax and the transfer tax.

Selling with taxes owed

First obtain the payoff from the Treasurer in writing, then set it beside a realistic sale price. A house in good condition may do fine on the open market, though that path involves preparation, showings and a buyer's financing. A house that needs work, or a June sale date that is close, makes a cash purchase as-is the faster option. Either way, the taxes owed are paid out of the price when you close.

Before talking to a buyer, collect the latest tax statement, the Assessor's parcel record and any repair or flood paperwork. Having them keeps surprises away from the closing table, and it gives you a clear answer to the first question any buyer asks, which is what is owed on the property. A clear answer early on keeps an offer from being renegotiated at the last minute, and it lets you decide with the real numbers in front of you rather than a guess.

Madison County at a glance

Winterset anchors Madison County, a south-central Iowa county of 16,548 people in 2020. It is the seat of government and the largest town at 5,353. Earlham follows at 1,410, then St. Charles (640), Truro (509), Patterson (176), East Peru (115), Macksburg (97) and Bevington (57, partly in Warren County).

The typical seller owns a small-town house or an acreage, not a subdivision lot, so a buyer judges the parcel and the town together. Weather history counts as well. A low-end EF4 tornado hit just outside Winterset on March 5, 2022. If you have repaired a roof after hail or wind, hold onto the invoices, since lenders and buyers will want to see them.

Who handles property tax

The Madison County Annex, 201 W. Court Avenue in Winterset, houses both offices you will deal with. One decides what your property is worth, which is the Assessor. The other sends the bill and takes the money, which is the Treasurer.

Values are redone every other year as of January 1. Farm ground is priced on its productive capacity instead of what neighbors paid. Maps and parcel records live on the county's assessor page, which links to the Beacon records site.

How to protest your assessment

Assessment notices arrive around April 1. You then have April 2 through April 30 to file a written protest. If you would rather talk first, the Assessor takes informal review requests from April 2 to April 25.

State law, Iowa Code 441.37, restricts a protest to five grounds:

  • Your value is out of step with comparable property nearby.
  • The figure is above the legal limit.
  • The parcel is exempt, can't be assessed, or sits in the wrong class.
  • Someone made an error in the assessment.
  • Fraud or misconduct occurred, and the protest has to spell it out.

Want to speak at a hearing? Say so in writing when you file. A disaster declaration for the county can move the filing period to May 1 through June 5.

The Board of Review

Three county residents make up the Board of Review: a farmer, a real estate broker and a contractor. The conference board names them. The Assessor does not direct how they vote.

Hearings start May 1 and are supposed to wrap up by May 31, unless the Department of Revenue grants more time. You should receive a written ruling that gives reasons. To go further, take the case to the Property Assessment Appeal Board or district court within 20 days of adjournment or May 31, whichever comes later (the Department of Revenue's board of review summary).

In odd-numbered years there is a second window, October 9 through October 31, for owners affected by a state equalization order. The sole argument then is that the order lifts the value above actual value.

Paying property tax and late interest

Iowa lets you settle the year in one payment or two. An unpaid half turns delinquent on October 1 or April 1. From then on, interest is one and one-half percent a month, rounded to the dollar, never under $1, and a partial month is billed as a full month (Iowa Code 445.39).

Walk in to the annex, mail a check to the Treasurer, or pay online. An elderly or disabled owner can apply for that homestead credit through the Treasurer by June 1 of each year (see the Madison County Treasurer site).

If the first half is still unpaid by February 1, a delinquency notice is mailed. A notice that never reaches you does not cancel what you owe.

When taxes go unpaid

Delinquent parcels must be offered by the treasurer at a yearly tax sale. It takes place the third Monday in June, barring good cause for a different June date (Iowa Code 446.7). The bid starts at the total of taxes, interest, fees and costs.

Even after the sale, the former owner may redeem. The payoff adds up the sale price, a certificate fee and two percent interest per month starting with the sale month, as set out in Iowa Code 447.1. Those months pile up, so clearing the balance before June is the cheaper route.

What a sale involves for taxes

Whoever records the deed with the county recorder must attach a declaration of value, which a buyer, seller or agent can sign. A copy then goes to the assessor, who files it for three years after the transfer year.

Iowa also charges a transfer tax of 80 cents per $500 of value above the first $500 (Iowa Code 428A.1). Nothing in the statute names the payer, which leaves it to your purchase contract.

The tax attaches to the parcel as a lien, so what is unpaid is normally taken out of your proceeds when you close. The homestead credit follows its own calendar. After a sale before July 1, the buyer files for the credit by July 1. After a sale past July 1, the credit stays put for that year (the Iowa administrative rule).

Before you sell with tax owed

Call the Treasurer at 515-462-1542 and ask for a payoff figure covering tax, interest and fees on each parcel. That number tells you what the sale has to clear.

  • Request the parcel record from the Assessor and look for wrong square footage or class while the April 30 window is open.

  • Report removed or damaged buildings to the Assessor, since owners must report those changes.
  • Before signing, put in writing who covers the transfer tax and the second-half tax.
  • Keep the Treasurer's receipt after closing as proof the parcel was clear.

Someone buying for cash as-is will not ask you to fix the roof or repaint, although liens and back taxes still come out at closing. With the June sale approaching, a cash sale may finish sooner than a listing would, and you avoid showings while it does.

Whichever route you take, bring a short folder to every conversation: the latest tax statement, the Treasurer's payoff figure, the parcel record and any repair invoices. A buyer, a title company or a closing agent will ask for these, and having them ready shortens the whole process by days.

What is the county seat of Madison County, Iowa?

Winterset, the largest city too, at 5,353 people in 2020. Both the Assessor and the Treasurer are in the Madison County Annex, 201 W. Court Avenue.

What is the deadline to protest a Madison County assessment?

The deadline is April 30 and filing opens April 2. Informal review with the Assessor is possible April 2 to April 25. A disaster declaration can push the deadline to June 5.

How often does Madison County revalue property?

Every second year, effective January 1. Owners should tell the Assessor about new construction, remodels, finished basements, decks and any buildings removed or damaged.

What happens if I miss the Madison County tax due date?

Interest of one and one-half percent a month begins once the October 1 or April 1 delinquency date passes. Parcels still unpaid may go to the June tax sale.

Who pays Iowa transfer tax when a Madison County house sells?

The rate is 80 cents per $500 above the first $500. The statute does not assign it to either side, so the purchase contract or local custom decides. Your closing agent can tell you which applies.

Fort Dodge and the local economy

Fort Dodge began as an army post in 1850, was renamed for Henry Dodge, and was incorporated in 1869. A gypsum mill opened in 1872, and gypsum and limestone mining remain part of the economy alongside biofuels, livestock feed, can production, drywall, trucking and veterinary pharmaceuticals.

US 20 runs through the middle of the county and skirts Fort Dodge on the south, and US 169 passes to the west. The latest estimate is 20,303, down a little from 20,816 in 2010.

The courthouse at 114 E. 6th Street houses both the treasurer and the assessor, which makes one trip enough for most property tax errands.

Who does what

Property tax passes through three hands here. The assessor decides what a parcel is worth, the auditor turns local budgets into rates, and the treasurer receives your check.

  • Carroll County Treasurer: ground floor of the courthouse, 114 E. 6th Street, Carroll, IA 51401. Phone 712-792-1200. Takes payments, chases delinquent accounts and runs the June auction.
  • Carroll County Assessor: under the same roof. The county has posted more than one phone number for this office, so try 712-792-9973 or check the county site before you drive over.
  • Board of Review: hears spring protests, with petitions filed through the assessor.
  • Iowa Department of Revenue: sets statewide rules and orders equalization between classes of property.

Reappraisal and new values

A full reappraisal is under way and wraps up December 31, 2026. The new numbers start January 1, 2027. The Conference Board approved the project in February 2022, and the county hired Vanguard Appraisals to do the fieldwork.

Appraisers record construction type, interior finish, condition, age and exterior measurements. They do not quote a value at the door. Final value notices go out after January 1, 2027, informal meetings are planned for spring 2027, and bills for fiscal 2028 and 2029 will use them.

Thinking of selling in the coming year? Today's bill still rests on the old valuation, and a buyer looking at a low figure could see a bigger one after the 2027 notices. Expect them to ask. A check or cash payment must land with the treasurer by the last business day before the delinquent month, or carry a timely postmark (Iowa Code 445.37). The statement is addressed to whoever holds title, whether or not a lender pays from escrow.

How the June tax sale works

Each year the county auctions unpaid taxes, normally the third Monday of June. Recent sales ran online through GovEase, with bids accepted from 9:00 to 10:30 a.m. People who want to bid sign up ahead of time and pay a $40 registration fee.

Bidding starts at 100 percent and moves down in whole percentages. The lowest percentage wins, and ties go to a random draw. Whoever wins covers the back taxes, interest and a $20 certificate fee. The owner can still redeem by repaying the sale amount with 2 percent added for each month.

Your petition, in writing, goes to the Board of Review sometime from April 2 through April 30 of the assessment year. Nobody on the board can stretch that window.

Iowa Code 441.37 allows five arguments: unfair comparison with similar property, a figure above legal value, an exemption or classification problem, a clerical error, or fraud. Ask the assessor for a petition form. The Property Assessment Appeal Board also describes each step online.

When the state orders equalization and your class goes up, a short second window opens October 9 to October 31. SF 2472, signed May 18, 2026, swapped the old homestead credit for an exemption beginning with assessment year 2026. It takes 10 percent off a home's taxable value, never less than $5,500 and never more than $20,000. Bills paid in September 2027 and March 2028 are the first to show it.

Anyone already claiming the credit stays enrolled without refiling. A new buyer files for their own claim.

City incentives for new construction

The city of Carroll runs an urban revitalization area that gives a five year exemption covering the first $75,000 of value added by improvements. Construction has to follow February 25, 2019 in the original area, or November 22, 2021 in the expanded area, and the project must raise assessed value by at least 10 percent.

The city also lists an Infill Housing Incentive of $20,000 per new owner-occupied home while funds last, and a speculative home loan program backed by five local banks. These programs favor new construction, so an older house competes with new homes that carry abatements and incentive money.

Selling with taxes and transfer tax in mind

Most sales credit the buyer with the seller's slice of the current tax at closing, and the settlement statement lays out the split.

A transfer tax of 80 cents per $500 over the first $500 also applies (Iowa Code 428A.1). Each deed travels with a declaration of value signed by a seller or a buyer. The recorder passes it to the assessor, who holds it three years. Who bears the tax is left to the purchase contract.

April 2 to April 30 of the assessment year, filed with the Board of Review. A second window, October 9 to October 31, exists only after a state equalization order raises your value.

Will my Carroll County property tax change after the reappraisal?

Possibly. The reappraisal's values begin January 1, 2027 and drive bills for fiscal 2028 and 2029, with notices arriving after that date.

Fayette County at a glance

Fayette County lies in northeastern Iowa. West Union holds the courthouse offices, while Oelwein is the biggest city at 5,920 people in 2020. If your mailing address says Sumner or Fairbank, the parcel could belong to another county, so confirm with the parcel record before you hunt for a statement.

With fewer people and older owners, the county sees plenty of inherited and empty houses, and those sellers often face tax, title and condition questions all at once.

West Union is home to both property tax offices: the Assessor decides values and the Treasurer takes payment. Doors are open weekdays, 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m.

Valuations can be searched on the Beacon mapping site. What you owe depends on assessed values and the budgets of schools, cities, the county, townships and community colleges.

Due dates and the assessor's calendar

The assessor revalues real property every second year and expects owners to report new buildings, decks, garages, additions and demolitions. Who sits on the Board of Review

The board has three or five people on staggered six-year terms. The Conference Board names them, and it is made up of the Board of Supervisors, the city mayors and one delegate per school district. The roster has to include a farmer, a real estate sales representative and someone from architecture or construction, with no more than two sharing a job.

Use the state form for a written protest, and base it on one of the five grounds in Iowa Code 441.37: unfairness next to similar property, a value over the legal figure, misclassification, a mistake, or fraud. Ask for a hearing when you file. Expect a written ruling that gives reasons.

Homestead exemption changes

The homestead credit is giving way to an exemption of 10 percent of taxable value, no lower than $5,500 and no higher than $20,000. Assessment year 2026 is the start, and September 2027 and March 2028 are the first payments to reflect it.

Under the old credit, owners got the tax on $4,850 of value knocked off. Those already enrolled stay enrolled, and the disabled veteran homestead credit continues. Whoever buys your house files for the exemption themselves, and July 1 is the cutoff. If your closing sits close to that date, ask the assessor how the claim is handled.

Selling a house with taxes due

At closing the year's tax is usually prorated, and anything delinquent gets paid first. Because Iowa taxes trail by a year, each bill pays for the fiscal year that ended the prior June 30.

Heirs make up a good share of local sellers. Begin at the treasurer's counter for a payoff covering this installment and any older balance. Armed with that, the title company can settle the tax at the table. Selling to a cash buyer as-is cuts out repair requests, yet the payoff and recording steps are identical.

Keeping the calendar straight

The assessment calendar and the payment calendar are two separate clocks. The first decides what your parcel is worth, and its deadlines fall in spring, with the equalization protests in October. The second decides when you pay, in September and March. A seller who mixes them up can miss a protest window while worrying about a bill, or the reverse. Write both sets of dates down before you list, and share them with your buyer so nobody is surprised later.

July 1 deserves a circle on the calendar for another reason. It is the filing deadline for the homestead credit, disabled veteran homestead credit and military exemption, so a buyer who closes in June has little time to file.

What to ask the assessor before listing

A short phone call to 563-422-3397 can answer several questions at once. Which year was the last revaluation, and when is the next one? Are all buildings, decks and garages on the record? Is a homestead credit attached, and what does a buyer need to do to claim their own? The Beacon site shows the valuation, and printing it for your buyer saves time during negotiation. If you are not sure whether your parcel sits in Fayette County at all, ask the same question about the county line before anything else, because a house near Sumner or Fairbank may belong to Bremer or Buchanan County and be billed there instead. No, every second year. The assessment date is January 1 and notices go out by April 1.

Yes. Money owed is normally paid from proceeds at closing, since delinquent amounts must be cleared for a clean transfer. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure.

Closing from July 1 through December 31 means you owe September. Closing from January 1 through June 30 means you owe March.

How to appeal your assessment

If the assessed value looks wrong, put a written protest in front of the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30. Hancock's board has five members and sits on or about May 1, and you are entitled to a written ruling with its reasons.

  • The figure is higher than the law permits.
  • The classification is wrong, or the parcel should be exempt.
  • Someone made a mistake in the assessment.
  • Fraud was involved.

A bare statement that the number seems high rarely succeeds. Gather values for a few comparable houses close to yours and submit them with the protest.

Hancock County winters punish roofs, furnaces and plumbing. Forest City averages about 40.2 inches of snow a year. An inspector going through an older small-town house usually flags the roof, insulation, the heating system and a damp basement. Buyers with a mortgage often want these repaired or the price cut.

An as-is cash purchase skips that negotiation. Liens, back taxes and open permits do not disappear, though. They are cleared at the closing table whichever way the house sells, so find out what is attached to your parcel early, and the sale will move faster for you and for whoever buys. The office is in the Courthouse at 855 State Street, Garner, Iowa 50438. It is open weekdays from 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and the phone number is 641-923-3122.

You pay the price the parcel sold for plus 2 percent interest for each month, using guaranteed funds. Ask the treasurer for an exact payoff figure.

Is Forest City in Hancock County?

Partly. The city spans Hancock and Winnebago counties, and the county containing your parcel decides which treasurer sends the bill.

What is the deadline to protest my Hancock County assessment?

The written protest goes to the Board of Review between April 2 and April 30. The board meets on or about May 1 and must answer in writing.

A practical order of steps

First, ask the treasurer what is owed and whether any half is already late. Second, find out whether the parcel is on the advertised list, since the advertising fee and the certificate fee both land on a parcel that sells. Third, confirm what the assessor has on file for buildings, because a deck, garage or addition that was never reported will surprise a buyer. Fourth, pull flood and insurance paperwork if the house is near the Turkey River or the Mississippi. Finally, send the title company a payoff figure so the tax comes out of proceeds at closing. If a bill reaches you after the sale, forward it, since the county mails to whoever held title when the statement was issued.

Selling an older house here

Clayton County houses range from river town limestone buildings to rural farmhouses, and many need roofs, wiring or foundation attention. Sellers who would rather not manage repairs can sell for cash as-is. The tax steps stay the same either way: confirm the balance, clear any penalty, and let the title company settle the county's share at the table.

Storms and what they did

The June 2008 flood followed 3 to 7 inches of rain over two days, closed roads with mudslides and caused more than $10 million in property damage. Beyond floods, the county has recorded 14 tornadoes since 1950, among them an F3 west of Elkader on May 30, 1985, and Elkader's snowfall averages about 37 inches a season.

None of this stops a sale, but buyers and their insurers ask about it. If your house sits low near a creek or river, having an elevation certificate or insurance history ready shortens the conversation and keeps the closing on track, and it signals to a buyer that the house has been looked after.

What to bring to the treasurer's window

Bring the parcel number or the property address, last year's statement if you have it, and a closing date or a rough one. With those, staff can quote what is owed on each installment, including any penalty already running, and tell you whether the parcel has been advertised for the June sale. If you are selling an inherited house, bring whatever document shows you can act for the owner, since the office will want to know who is asking. Ask for the figure in writing, and ask how long it stays good, because the penalty grows monthly and a number quoted today will be too low in a few weeks.

A seller who lives out of the area can usually handle this by phone at 563-245-1106 and then pass the figure to the title company.

Frequently asked questions

When are Clayton County property taxes due?

The first installment is due September 1 and the second March 1. Penalties of 1 1/2 percent a month start the following October 1 and April 1.

Where do I pay property tax in Clayton County?

Go to the County Treasurer in Elkader, 111 High Street NE, Suite 102, or call 563-245-1106 on a weekday between 8:00 a.m. and 4:00 p.m.

When is the Clayton County tax sale?

Third Monday of June, 1:00 p.m. Parcels pay a $4.00 advertising fee ahead of the sale, plus $10.00 per certificate if one sells.

What is the protest deadline in Clayton County?

The window opens April 2 and closes April 30 under Iowa Code 441.37.

Which Clayton County areas flood?

Record floods hit the Turkey River at Elkader in June 2008 and the Mississippi at Guttenberg in April 1965. Check a property's flood zone before you list.
